description_full: Gaming and Leisure Properties, Inc. is engaged in the business of acquiring, financing, and owning real estate property to be leased to gaming operators in triple-net lease arrangements, pursuant to which the tenant is responsible for all facility maintenance, insurance required in connection with the leased properties and the business conducted on the leased properties, taxes levied on or with respect to the leased properties and all utilities and other services necessary or appropriate for the leased properties and the business conducted on the leased properties. Gaming and Leisure Properties, Inc. was established on February 13th, 2013, incorporated in 2013 in Pennsylvania in and is based in Wyomissing, United States.

financial_summary: Gaming and Leisure Properties,  is a large-cap real estate business with a $11.6B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +4.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 7% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $825M in free cash flow — roughly 52 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.37× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 7.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 4.0% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 3.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 7% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 22% below the high.

val: The stock trades 49% below its DCF fair value of $75.80, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 27%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $54.39 to $108 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 11% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $49.37 on average, 27% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 6.5%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.63).
It converts 52% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.37x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 52%.

hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.9x net debt to EBITDA ($165.8M of cash against $7.2B of debt), with interest covered 3.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.10 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.7% over 3 years, 6.7% over 5 years and 10.7% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 44%).
At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 0.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 21.4% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 19.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.0%, and institutions hold 96%.

It returns 7.5% a year to shareholders (8.4% in dividends).
The share count has grown 3.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 30.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 20 employees, each generates about $79.7M of revenue, 34.9x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 17.0% a year.
That works out to $41.2M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.5M (0x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
